architect_action: Hold implementation and put this decision packet to the human. These are product decisions; no agent may answer them for them. Every lens that produced evidence ran on one provider, so this panel's agreement is one vendor's opinion counted several times.

human_signoff.rationale: The owner explicitly requested implementing the first agreed step: a shared Rust bridge cache on main without reducing checks, passing CI and verifying merge-queue reuse and speed. Authorization is limited to this bounded scope, preserved protections and normal PR/queue delivery; no ruleset intervention, secret change or unrelated PR mutation is authorized.

product_decisions.affected_acceptance: FR-001 and SC-001 require both main-scoped entries to exist, the Edge Cases section accepts eviction, and plan.md:18 currently forbids deleting existing caches; the decision determines the lifecycle and rollback contract.
options: Accept the platform-managed GitHub Actions cache lifecycle, document the current retention/eviction rule and settings, and keep account export and purge N/A because entries contain no user data.

Set an owner-defined maximum lifetime independent of the platform default; the implementing agent chooses the cleanup mechanism, while account export and purge remain N/A for these non-personal artifacts.
product_decisions.question: Should the shared main-scoped compiler caches use GitHub Actions' platform-managed retention and eviction unchanged, or must BrainBuddy impose an explicit shorter maximum lifetime?
product_decisions.why_needed: The feature introduces durable repository cache records but specifies neither their retention period nor deletion trigger. Retention periods are product privacy decisions; cleanup mechanics remain with the implementing agent.

reviewers.summary: The cache outcome is generally consistent across the artifacts, but the release plan contradicts the accepted ASK landing contract and does not preserve exact-SHA review evidence across its two-PR merge-queue sequence.

The cache identity, variants, paths, data ownership, and rollback model align with current consumers. Changes are required because the ASK landing sequence contradicts binding repository controls, and cache-outage fallback is promised but absent from the unchanged consumers.

The success-path evidence and serial implementation → warm → merge-group verification lanes are otherwise proportionate, but two gaps prevent approval: the planned ASK landing cannot occur under the accepted controls, and the focused workflow-contract test is neither included in exact-SHA CI nor scoped to every accepted operational failure mode. No product decision is needed.

Consent, owner scoping, 404-vs-403 behavior, and account-data authorization are N/A because this feature adds no product API or user-content path. The proposed workflow is least-privilege and caches only source-derived compiler artifacts. However, a cold producer run will emit an absolute runner-local path in GitHub logs, violating Constitution Principle I, and the new main-scoped caches lack an explicit retention, deletion, purge, and export disposition. The retention period requires a product privacy decision.

This lens does not apply. The artifacts consistently constrain the feature to trusted CI cache preparation, explicitly declare no user-visible surface and no impact on mobile workflows, and introduce no product loading, empty, error, partial-failure, keyboard, focus, destructive-action, or interruption/resume behavior to specify.

technical_findings.description: The plan correctly classifies the workflow change as ASK, but then requires normal PR/merge-queue landing and explicitly says that no ruleset intervention is planned. The accepted landing contract says every `.github/` change is ASK and, while the landing deploy key remains the sole bypass actor, neither a PR nor a direct human push can update main without the recorded temporary ruleset intervention. The follow-up documentation PR also cannot produce the required real merge-group evidence under those stated protections. This leaves the planned acceptance sequence without a valid landing path and conflicts with the specification's unqualified assertion that existing protections are preserved.

technical_findings.recommendation: Revise the specification and plan to name a governance-compliant landing and restoration sequence for every planned PR: explicit recorded approval, green required CI on the exact landing SHA, audited temporary ruleset intervention, and evidence that protections were restored. If repository settings now provide a separately accountable merge path, first reconcile the accepted ADR and runbook with that current state and cite the evidence instead of asserting a queue-only path.

The later documentation PR advances the repository again and has no independent exact-SHA review step. Consequently, the plan does not establish that the reviewed, tested, landed, and deployed SHA are identical, and the first PR's review cannot cover the final documentation commit.

technical_findings.recommendation: Define an exact-SHA evidence sequence for each repository-changing step. Freeze the actual SHA that will land, obtain independent review and required CI for that same SHA, verify main equals it, and retain deployment evidence. Treat the follow-up documentation commit as a new SHA requiring its own applicable gate; do not reuse the workflow PR's review as evidence for it.

technical_findings.description: The specification promises that a cache outage retains the cold-build path, but the plan keeps existing consumers unchanged. Both Apple consumers currently invoke actions/cache@v6 without an error-tolerant recovery boundary. A restore exception fails that step, so the subsequent bridge-build step does not run; only an ordinary cache miss reaches the cold build. Warming failure and eviction handling do not satisfy the broader outage requirement.
evidence: specs/035-shared-rust-bridge-cache/spec.md:18-19 explicitly includes cache outage in the cold-build guarantee.
specs/035-shared-rust-bridge-cache/plan.md:6-7 says existing consumers remain unchanged and only describes exact misses.
specs/035-shared-rust-bridge-cache/plan.md:17-18 covers warming failure and eviction but not consumer restore errors.
.github/workflows/ci.yml:995-1014 shows the full Apple consumer's cache action followed by a cold build only when cache-hit is not true.
.github/workflows/ci.yml:1140-1160 has the same behavior for the Mac-only variant.
[actions/cache v6 restoreImpl.ts](https://github.com/actions/cache/blob/v6/src/restoreImpl.ts#L79-L84) marks restore exceptions as step failures with core.setFailed.
technical_findings.recommendation: Extend the plan's owned scope to provide an explicit consumer-side restore-error fallback for both Apple variants. It must remove or avoid partially restored output before cold compilation and retain required-check failure for genuine build/test failures. Add focused verification for this failure path; an exact cache miss test alone is insufficient.

technical_findings.description: The plan introduces a focused semantic test for the new workflow, but neither required exact-SHA CI nor make validate-ci invokes that test. The stated test scope also omits explicit assertions for the accepted concurrency, cancellation, and failed-warm isolation safeguards. Full CI could therefore pass while the new test is never executed or while those operational invariants are absent.

Record its passing result for the frozen SHA.

technical_findings.description: The planned cache-miss path invokes the existing bridge script unchanged, and that script deterministically writes its absolute KIT directory to the GitHub Actions log. Constitution Principle I forbids local file paths in logs, so the first successful warming run would violate a binding MUST.

technical_findings.description: The feature creates two new main-scoped durable cache entries, but the artifacts mention eviction without defining the retention source of truth, deletion trigger, or lifetime. They also do not explicitly state that these non-personal build artifacts are outside account export and account purge and may survive an account purge. Because the contents are limited to compiler artifacts and generated bindings, this is not currently a GDPR erasure gap, but the disposition cannot remain implicit.
